description: PasswordsCon talks from BSides Las Vegas 2023.

talks.title: The attackers guide to exploiting secrets in the universe
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers find and exploit leaked credentials in git repositories, container images and mobile apps.
talks.summary:
Secrets such as API keys, cloud credentials and certificates are meant to be used by software rather than people, yet they keep turning up in source code, images and apps. The talk looks at how attackers find them and why one valid credential can provide initial access or let an intruder keep a foothold after getting inside.

The first part covers public and private git repositories. Activity on public GitHub is broadcast through a readable events feed, which can expose pushes and repositories that were made public with old history still attached. A planted honey token was tried by unknown callers within a short time. Exposed .git directories on web servers can be pulled back into full repositories, and private source code often carries credentials buried in its branch history. The second part looks at container images and compiled applications. Images on Docker Hub and Android and iOS packages are archives that can be unpacked and scanned, and a meaningful share of them were found to contain plaintext secrets. A supply chain incident involving a code coverage tool illustrated how a credential in a public image can lead into private repositories.

The practical takeaways are to stop hardcoding credentials, adopt a secrets manager the team can realistically roll out, run automated secret detection in repositories and pipelines, install git hooks, rotate keys regularly and grant each key only the privileges it needs. Restricting which machines may use a key also limits what a stolen one can do.

talks.title: How to Handle Getting Dumped: Compromised Passwords
talks.teaser: Explains where stolen passwords from malware dumps come from, how to triage them, and how to respond when accounts appear.
talks.summary:
Compromised passwords often arrive as part of malware dumps from infostealers, and this talk explains how an organization can respond when its accounts appear in them. The speaker, a threat hunter and incident responder, outlines where these dumps circulate, including infostealer families, underground Telegram channels, breach-notification services and initial access brokers. Commodity stealers collect much more than passwords, such as browser history, cookies, saved form data, screenshots and sometimes cryptocurrency wallet material, and their logs can be detailed enough to rival endpoint telemetry. Costs and pitfalls also come up: subscriptions and broker fees run from hundreds to thousands of dollars, data may be stale or fabricated, and some entries hold hashes rather than plaintext.

The middle section turns to triage and response. Teams should first confirm that the usernames are real, then check whether the password still works, review whether the host is a corporate or personal device, and examine the source IP details. Response planning covers locking accounts, forcing resets, cleaning the device so reinfection does not occur, and preparing messages for users and their managers. If a credential is confirmed valid, authentication logs and second-factor logs should be reviewed for unusual logins.

The closing advice focuses on prevention and detection. Organizations should discourage browser-stored passwords, promote password managers, favor strong multifactor authentication such as hardware keys, keep endpoints patched, and train SOC analysts to recognize credential-stealing malware rather than treating it as an ordinary infection. Legal and policy questions, such as whether to buy data from brokers or vendors, should be settled before an incident occurs.

talks.title: Are your secrets safe - How mobile applications are leaking millions of credentials
talks.teaser: Shows how hardcoded API keys and credentials end up inside Android and iOS apps, and how to find them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that machine-to-machine credentials such as API keys, certificates and service tokens are often hardcoded or left in the wrong place, because people handle them even though systems use them. Mobile apps make this worse, since a simple app usually connects to many third-party services, and each connection needs its own secret.

The speaker looks at public GitHub data, where a yearly GitGuardian report counted about 10 million validated secrets in 2023, and notes that mobile-specific files such as Android manifests, strings.xml and iOS plist files appear often in leaks. The talk then walks through downloading Android and iOS apps, decompiling the APK and unzipping the IPA, and scanning the extracted code. The live scan found valid Google API keys, Slack webhooks and other service credentials in a store app. A penetration test on a bank app is described, where a hardcoded S3 bucket credential exposed thousands of stored check images. Third-party studies of Play Store apps are also summarised, with a large share containing hardcoded credentials.

The takeaways are that secrets belong on the server side behind a login, since obfuscation, Base64 encoding and splitting keys do not protect them. Where a key must live in the app, it should be tightly scoped, restricted by IP or service, and paired with app signing. Teams should assume source code will be read, scan repositories and builds for secrets, and rotate credentials on a regular schedule.

talks.title: Password911: Authentication Adventures in Healthcare
talks.teaser: Examines authentication problems in clinical settings, from shared infusion pump keys to hardcoded service codes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why passwords and authentication are hard to get right in hospitals, where a locked-out clinician or an unreachable device can directly affect patient care. Matt Weir frames the problem around clinical workflows, arguing that security controls cannot simply get in the way of treatment.

Through case studies, he walks through controlled substance infusion pumps, which often share one lock key across manufacturers, and pacemakers, whose pairing depends on serial-number-based PINs and whose programmers must work offline. He also covers a vulnerability where Wi-Fi credentials were stored unencrypted in flash memory. He found credentials on some purchased equipment, though not on the pump model he opened. Other examples include firmware updates with no signing, service PIN codes listed in manuals, hardcoded remote passwords, and patient apps that verify who a user is but not what that user may access.

His takeaways are that medical devices should be assessed as a whole system, that resilience matters when keys leak, and that threat modeling and standard guidance help manufacturers who lack security staff. He argues the goal is making secure options easy to adopt, while keeping break-glass access available when care depends on it.

talks.title: Policies, Securing, Cracking, and More
talks.teaser: Explains how Active Directory and Entra ID password policies actually apply, and how weak passwords get attacked and cracked.
talks.summary:
Derek Melber starts from the premise that passwords will remain in Windows environments, especially for service accounts that cannot use multi-factor authentication. He explains how Active Directory password policy really applies: it must be linked to the domain to govern domain users, while a policy linked to an organizational unit only reaches local accounts on the computers inside it. Fine-grained password policy objects allow different rules for different groups, ordered by priority, and he shows a PowerShell check to reveal the policy a user actually receives.

The talk then contrasts this with Entra ID, where most password settings cannot be tuned. Defaults include an eight-character minimum and no expiry unless enabled, plus a banned-word list maintained by Microsoft and a custom list capped at 1,000 words. On the attack side he covers phishing, pass-the-hash and ticket abuse, and password spraying versus brute force, including how lockout thresholds can be exploited. He demonstrates cracking with dictionary, brute-force and rainbow-table methods.

He closes with defensive advice: disable LM and NTLMv1 where possible, since NTLMv2 and Kerberos are hard to remove. Length matters most, so passphrases of 20 or more characters are preferable, and security teams should make sure password spraying reaches their monitoring.

talks.title: Trusted Devices: Unlocking a Password Manager without a password
talks.teaser: Explains how a password manager can derive its decryption key from SSO sign-ins or passkeys, and the design changes that requires.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a practical design question for password managers: if a user signs in with single sign-on or a passkey, where does the key that unlocks the vault come from? The speakers, both from 1Password, explain that federated identity supplies a strong assertion of who someone is but no cryptographic material. Their answer pairs that assertion with a key stored on the user's device.

The middle of the talk covers the mechanics. New devices must be approved by a trusted device already signed in. A short code shown on both screens feeds a balanced password-authenticated key exchange, which lets the server relay messages without being able to read the credentials passed between devices. Device keys cannot decrypt vault items directly, so an intermediate layer of keys sits between them. Offline unlock depends on platform secure storage: iOS, Android and recent macOS offer hardware-backed options, while Linux and Windows keep material in kernel-protected memory. Windows TPMs were described as poorly documented and sometimes unreliable for this purpose.

The closing section weighed trade-offs. A copied device credential can be reused elsewhere, a risk businesses already accept with single sign-on, and admins want per-vault rules that limit access by hardware quality. The speakers' takeaway is that removing the master password moves the security question onto the device, so passwordless designs need strong device controls, careful fallbacks and clear policy choices.

talks.title: Could Passwordless be Worse than Passwords?
talks.teaser: Shows how flaws in passwordless WebAuthn logins can enable account takeover, plus fixes for developers and testers.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether passwordless login, including WebAuthn-based passkeys, security keys and biometrics, can end up less secure than the passwords it replaces. It begins with background on what passwordless means, how magic links and one-time codes differ from it, and why large vendors are pushing it. The speaker then argues that the protocol is rarely the weak point; the surrounding web application is.

Several real flaws are walked through. In one case the server accepted a username in a registration request that the client could change, letting an attacker attach a new device to another account, including an executive's. A magic-link flow exposed admin access through a simple change to the URL, and a multi-step challenge flow allowed parameter tampering that logged a user in as someone else. A demo application also let attackers register devices to existing accounts because it never checked whether a user already existed.

The closing advice targets developers, testers, enterprises and end users. Developers should validate every value server-side rather than trusting what the specification passes through, and protect every endpoint. Testers should focus on parameter tampering and unauthenticated APIs instead of the cryptography. Organizations should question vendors about testing, bug bounty programs and disclosure. Users have little defence against device-adding attacks, and account recovery often still falls back to passwords, a gap that remains open.

talks.title: How I Met Your Printer
talks.teaser: Shows how office printers leak stored credentials that can be used to move deeper into a corporate network.
talks.summary:
Tom Pohl, a penetration testing team manager, argues that office printers are a common and overlooked way into corporate networks. Many of the printers he meets during internal tests still use default credentials, and when those fail he looks for other routes, such as a hidden supervisor account with a blank password on some Ricoh models.

The talk walks through several pass-back techniques, where the device is tricked into sending its own stored credentials to an attacker-controlled listener. Examples include pointing the LDAP address lookup setting at a fake server and using the built-in test button, and changing the SMTP server and enabling automatic email alerts so the printer sends its mail login out. Scan-to-folder settings can be redirected to an attacker-controlled share to capture NTLMv2 hashes, which can then be cracked offline. Stored SMTP credentials were also shown to grant access to a mailbox holding scanned documents from across an organization. The talk also covers similar weaknesses in server management interfaces and room control systems.

For defenders, the recommendations are to segment management interfaces, change every default account, require encrypted authentication, use app-specific passwords or tightly scoped service accounts, and forward device logs to a central logging system. Tom closes by noting that any networked device storing credentials can be exposed in the same way.

talks.title: Do you know where your secrets are? Exploring the problem of secret sprawl
talks.teaser: Presents research on hardcoded credential leaks in public GitHub and a five-level maturity model for secret management.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with breaches linked to credentials left in code or environments, including Uber, CircleCI and Toyota, and argues that exposed secrets are a recurring step in attackers moving laterally and escalating privileges. The speaker frames the problem as secret sprawl: credentials copied into source repositories, CI pipelines, logs and storage buckets, often during debugging and rarely removed afterward.

The middle section walks through data from scanning public GitHub commits. Figures cited include roughly 10 million newly detected hardcoded credentials in a single year, a 67 percent rise, and about 5.5 secrets for every thousand commits. Google API keys made up most detections, while OpenAI keys were the fastest-growing category in the current year. A survey of IT decision makers found that most had experienced a leak in the previous 18 months, and many relied only on manual code review to catch them.

The closing part presents a five-level secret management maturity model, from hardcoding credentials at the bottom to dynamic, short-lived secrets with automated rotation and continuous monitoring at the top. It rests on three pillars: people, processes and tools. Practical takeaways include scoping credentials narrowly, moving them into a vault, scanning at commit, pull request and build stages, and treating network egress controls as part of the defense. The speaker encouraged teams to assess their current level and plan the next step.
